Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette:
Karim Al-Farsi, a 78-year-old roofer, had always prided himself on his steady hands and sharp focus, qualities essential for his trade. But that changed two years ago during a renovation project at a local community center. He was on the roof, overseeing a new sealant application, when a faulty ventilation system below unexpectedly released a plume of highly corrosive chemicals. The immediate horror wasn't just the burning in his lungs, but the screams from the playground adjacent to the building, where children were gathered for an after-school program. He had seen paramedics rush in, their faces grim, and though he later learned no children were seriously harmed, the image of their panicked scattering became etched into his mind.

In the months that followed, Karim found himself increasingly trapped in a cycle of fear. He was plagued by the memory of the incident, which would force its way into his mind at the most unwelcome times. He might be having dinner with his wife, or trying to focus on a new roofing bid, and suddenly, the distinct sensation of burning chemicals and the sound of distant screams would overwhelm him, even without any clear image or memory of the event itself. Yet, paradoxically, when he tried to deliberately recall the specifics of what happened-the exact sequence, the faces of the emergency responders-he found it strangely difficult to access the memory. This constant, unbidden intrusion of past sensations, rather than a clear narrative, meant that his mind was always primed to find connections, making seemingly innocuous details in his environment suddenly potent reminders.

This constant, unbidden intrusion of the past made Karim live in a perpetual state of alarm. He was unable to relax even in the comfort of his own home, his muscles taut, his senses on high alert. This pervasive sense of impending danger meant that his body was always primed for a threat, making him startle violently at the slightest unexpected touch, like his wife's gentle hand on his shoulder. His sleep, once a deep, restorative refuge, became fragmented and fitful, leaving him exhausted and even more on edge.

This heightened state of threat, this inability to relax, paradoxically amplified his sensitivity to anything that might remind him of the event. He found himself scanning constantly, hyper-vigilant for signs of danger, which meant that mundane observations morphed into potent triggers. If he saw children playing in the park across the street, their innocent shouts would immediately activate the memory of the community center incident, bringing back the chemical smell and the terror. Similarly, catching snippets of related news on the television-even a report about local air quality or industrial accidents-would instantly unlock those distressing recollections. He even began to avoid certain known people, particularly those who had been involved in the clean-up or the subsequent investigations, because their presence alone would prompt an uncontrolled access of those painful, emotionally charged memories.

The more these memories forced their way into his mind, the more convinced he became that danger was everywhere, further intensifying his pervasive sense of threat and making him even more susceptible to triggers. His work, once a source of pride, became a battleground. He found himself hesitant on ladders, constantly looking over his shoulder, his concentration shattered by intrusive thoughts. He turned down larger projects, fearing the complex chemical applications. His wife, worried by his increasing withdrawal and constant jumpiness, encouraged him to seek help. Karim, though hesitant, finally agreed, hoping to find a way to quiet the constant storm in his mind, to regain some semblance of peace before the memories and the fear consumed him entirely.
